tasks.extracted: 35 trials, 75 observations, 3079 patients on methylphenidate and 2606 on placebo; pooled relative risks insomnia 1.61 (z = 9.2), initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6), middle insomnia 2.97 (z printed as 183), combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4), sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2), all p < 0.001.

tasks.page: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders; Figure 2
tasks.locator: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
tasks.extracted: Adjusted relative risks for insomnia in individual trials ranged widely: more than 75% not significantly different from 1, some significantly below 1 and some above 1; Egger's test t = 0.37, p = 0.7.

tasks.page: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Discussion
tasks.locator: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Drug and placebo adverse-event rates were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p < 0.0001) and observed relative risks were close to those predicted from the placebo rate alone; eliciting adverse events with questionnaires gives higher absolute rates but smaller relative risks than spontaneous reporting, so relative risks should be read with absolute risks, which the review does not report in its text.

Manuscript development funded by Ironshore Pharmaceuticals, whose product is among those compared; two Ironshore employees assisted with data extraction and two authors are employees of its parent company, Highland Therapeutics.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3, treatment column
tasks.extracted: MDMA against placebo (df 1 and 6): total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, reduced on the treatment night only (interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); no effect on wake after sleep onset, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).

tasks.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table 3
tasks.extracted: On the treatment night, REM percentage after MDMA was lower than after both shortened sleep (19.3%; P = 0.004) and placebo (P = 0.004) (F(2,12) = 15.036), which the authors read as a specific REM-suppressing effect beyond sleep loss.

tasks.locator: Table 3, recovery column; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Recovery night with placebo after the MDMA session: total sleep 403.6 (SEM 34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), against 431.9 minutes and 20.6% on the recovery night of the placebo session; no main effects of night apart from the REM interaction.

tasks.locator: Methods › Experimental Procedures, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph; Abstract › Measurements and Results
tasks.extracted: Only 7 completed; two withdrew and the 12-sequence Latin square was incomplete; the laboratory schedule was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times. The abstract states that MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, which the drug comparison does not show (P = 0.119).

tasks.page: Results › Effects on the MSLT; Figure 4
tasks.locator: Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Treatment by day interaction F = 4.63 (df 2 and 12), P = 0.032; after shortened sleep the mean nap-test latency was shorter than after placebo (about 6 minutes, per the Discussion), while after MDMA it differed neither from placebo nor from shortened sleep; no differences on the day after the recovery night; sleep-onset REM periods 2.14 (shortened sleep), 1.43 (MDMA), 1.00 (placebo), not significant.

tasks.locator: Abstract › Measurements and Results and Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors conclude that MDMA's sleep loss was not associated with next-day sleepiness and that next-day sleep latency remained at placebo levels; with 7 participants, MDMA's next-day values were not significantly different from those after shortened sleep either.

tasks.page: Results › Time-course of drug effects; Figure 1
tasks.locator: Results › Time-course of drug effects; Figure 1 legend
tasks.extracted: Effects generally significant by the first post-dose test, maximal over the following tests and decreasing at the last; DXM produced longer-lasting Balance and Circular Lights deficits than triazolam; at the penultimate and maximum DXM doses, deficits were still apparent at the last assessment; the highest doses sometimes produced complete impairment (scored 0).

No vomiting after placebo, triazolam or the two lowest DXM doses; 2 of 12 vomited at the third dose level and 7 of 12 at the fourth level or above; vomiting at one dose did not always predict vomiting at the next.

tasks.page: Abstract; Materials and Methods › General Procedures
tasks.locator: Abstract › Results; Materials and Methods › General Procedures, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The abstract states that drug effects resolved without significant adverse effects by the end of the session; the end-of-session measures, taken when acute effects were judged to have resolved, were questionnaires, and psychomotor tasks were last given at the final in-session test.

tasks.page: Materials and Methods › General Procedures; Data Analysis
tasks.locator: Materials and Methods › General Procedures, 5th paragraph; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Doses within each drug always rose and escalation stopped when a person could not complete a psychomotor and a computer task, or when the participant or investigator judged a higher dose inadvisable; data were missing at stop-point sessions.

tasks.page: Results › Measures assessed 1 month after drug administration › Persisting Effects Questionnaire
tasks.locator: Results › Measures assessed 1 month after drug administration › Persisting Effects Questionnaire, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: About one month after the final session: positive changes in attitudes about life and self, mood, social effects, behaviour and spirituality at 46% to 61% of maximum scores, negative ratings low; 4 of 12 rated the experiences among the five most meaningful of their lives and 7 of 12 among the five most spiritually significant; all 12 reported increased well-being (1 slightly, 7 moderately, 4 very much). The questionnaire could not separate DXM from triazolam sessions; in interviews, effects were attributed to sessions thought to be a classic hallucinogen.

One participant reached a stop point after a post-session headache attributed to DXM; the primary monitor was reachable by phone throughout, no volunteer called or reported distress after the sessions, and no lasting distress or persisting perceptual phenomena were reported at the one-month follow-up.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph; Materials and Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors note that volunteers knew the laboratory's psilocybin research and may have expected psilocybin, and that preparation, social support and the setting may have shaped their positive ratings; people with a personal or immediate-family history of schizophrenia, bipolar, delusional, paranoid or schizoaffective disorder were excluded.
